blocks.text: Here are the basic types of polarization of light.
When the electric field vector oscillates in a single plane, the light is said to be linearly polarized (Fig. 8.4a). An example is light passing through a polarizing filter, as in sunglasses.

When the electric field rotates circularly, either clockwise (right-handed) or anticlockwise (left-handed), the light is said to be circularly polarized (Fig. 8.4b). An example is light reflected off a CD (Compact Disc) or DVD (Digital Versatile Disc).

A combination of linear and circular polarization, in which the electric field vector traces an elliptical path, is called elliptical polarization. In elliptical polarization (Fig. 8.4c) the two components of the electric field, E_x and E_y, are not equal, and/or they differ in phase by an arbitrary angle theta. An example is light passing through a stress plate or a waveplate.

blocks.alt: A wave travelling along the x axis. The red electric field vectors all point up or down in one vertical plane, tracing a sine curve. A note says E always lies in the same plane.
blocks.caption: Linear polarization (original diagram after Figure 8.4a).

blocks.alt: Looking along the direction of travel, red electric field vectors from the centre end on a purple ellipse, turning as the wave moves. One vector is split into components Ex along x and Ey along y. A note says that when Ex and Ey are unequal the tip of E traces an ellipse.
blocks.caption: Elliptical polarization with components Ex and Ey (original diagram after Figure 8.4c).
